Hysteroscopy (when concurrent intrauterine lesions such as polyps or adhesions are suspected)
avoid: Plain abdominal radiography alone (no diagnostic value for pelvic soft-tissue lesions)
Routine full-panel tumor marker screening (unless malignancy is highly suspected, it readily leads to overtreatment)
Blind antibiotic treatment (should not be used as a routine diagnostic measure when there is no evidence of infection)

first_line: First-line treatment mainly consists of medications that suppress ovulation and lower estrogen levels. Commonly used nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) include ibuprofen 400mg 3 times daily, started 1-2 days before menstruation

or oral short-acting contraceptives (such as drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol), taken continuously or cyclically for 3-6 months. For patients with suspected endometriosis, progestins (such as dienogest 2mg/day) or GnRH-a injections may be considered. Nonpharmacologic interventions such as warm compresses and moderate exercise are also recommended.
safety_warnings: NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with active peptic ulcer disease, severe renal impairment, or a history of aspirin-induced asthma.
Oral contraceptives are contraindicated in smokers older than 35 years, those with a history of venous thromboembolism, or those with migraine with aura.
Long-term GnRH-a use may cause hypoestrogenic adverse effects (such as hot flashes and decreased bone mineral density), and add-back therapy should be considered.
personalization: For patients seeking fertility: avoid long-term ovulation suppression; prioritize NSAIDs or short-term progestins, and refer for surgery early if necessary.
For patients not seeking fertility with severe symptoms: long-term oral contraceptives or placement of a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (Mirena) may be considered.
Perimenopausal women: use hormone therapy cautiously, closely monitor breast and endometrial changes, and add androgen opposition if necessary.

skills.presentation: The patient previously had regular menstrual cycles and now has amenorrhea for more than 3 cycles or more than 6 months. It is often accompanied by hypoestrogenic symptoms such as hot flashes and night sweats, or hyperandrogenic manifestations such as galactorrhea, hirsutism, and acne. Some patients may have cyclic lower abdominal pain (suggesting genital tract obstruction) or headache and visual changes (suggesting pituitary disease). Recent weight changes, psychological stress, and medication history should be specifically elicited to help identify the cause.

first_questions: When was your last menstrual period? Were your periods regular before that?
Have you recently had significant weight loss, excessive exercise, or increased psychological stress?
Have you had nipple discharge outside breastfeeding, headache, or blurred vision?
followup_questions: If hirsutism or acne is present, ask further: 'Did these body hair changes appear suddenly in recent months?'
If there is galactorrhea, ask further: 'Does the discharge occur spontaneously or only with squeezing? Is it milky white?'
If pregnancy is suspected, ask further: 'Have you had unprotected sexual intercourse recently? Have you already done a urine pregnancy test yourself?'
stop_conditions: Pregnancy has been clearly excluded and amenorrhea has been confirmed to last more than 6 months.
A complete menstrual history, reproductive history, and recent weight change record have been obtained.
The patient has described typical associated symptoms (such as galactorrhea or hirsutism) sufficient to initially localize the cause.

essential: Serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) measurement
Six sex hormone panel (FSH, LH, E2, P, T, PRL)
Thyroid function tests (TSH, FT4)
if_suspected: Pelvic ultrasonography (to assess endometrial thickness and ovarian morphology)
Pituitary MRI (when hyperprolactinemia or pituitary adenoma is suspected)
Progesterone withdrawal test (to assess endogenous estrogen levels and uterine response)
avoid: Blind use of progesterone to induce withdrawal bleeding before pregnancy is excluded
Hysteroscopy without an indication (unless intrauterine adhesions are highly suspected and other tests cannot confirm the diagnosis)
Routine chromosome karyotype analysis (unless FSH is markedly elevated and age is <40 years)

first_line: Treatment should be directed at the underlying cause. For hypothalamic amenorrhea, lifestyle intervention is first-line (increased caloric intake, reduced exercise, and stress relief), with estrogen-progestin sequential therapy added if necessary to establish artificial cycles. For polycystic ovary syndrome, metformin combined with short-acting oral contraceptives is preferred to regulate menstruation. For hyperprolactinemia, bromocriptine or dopamine agonists are preferred. All patients require regular bone mineral density monitoring to prevent osteoporosis.
safety_warnings: Before estrogen use, breast cancer, a history of thrombosis, and unexplained vaginal bleeding must be excluded.
Bromocriptine may cause nausea and dizziness; starting at a low dose and taking it with food is recommended to prevent hypotension.
Long-term high-dose glucocorticoid use may cause Cushing syndrome and requires strict monitoring.
personalization: In adolescent patients, avoid potent ovulation-suppressing drugs and focus on nutritional support.
In perimenopausal women, use estrogen replacement therapy cautiously and assess cardiovascular risk.
For patients seeking fertility, long-acting contraception is contraindicated, and ovulation induction is preferred.

skills.presentation: Patients are mostly postmenopausal women who complain of vaginal dryness, burning, or dyspareunia. There is often thin, pale yellow, or purulent discharge, occasionally with a small amount of bloody leukorrhea. Some patients have urinary irritative symptoms such as urinary frequency and urgency. Symptoms often worsen after fatigue or sexual intercourse, with no obvious vulvar pruritus or only mild discomfort.

first_questions: Have you reached menopause? Have you recently had vaginal dryness or pain during sexual intercourse?
Have there been any changes in the color, character, or amount of your discharge? Is there any odor or blood streaking?
followup_questions: Do you have urinary symptoms such as frequency, urgency, or difficulty urinating?
Have you recently used topical medications or hormone replacement therapy?
stop_conditions: Menopausal status is clear and typical symptoms (dryness, yellow watery discharge) are clearly described.
Recent abnormal bleeding or high-risk factors for malignancy have been excluded.
The patient has no signs of severe systemic infection or complex comorbidities requiring further investigation.

essential: Gynecologic pelvic examination (to observe vaginal mucosal atrophy and hyperemia)
Routine vaginal discharge testing (pH measurement and microscopy)
Cervical cytology (TCT) to exclude cervical lesions
if_suspected: Colposcopy (if suspicious ulcers or masses are found)
Pelvic ultrasonography (to assess endometrial thickness and adnexa)
Six sex hormone panel testing (to help assess the degree of ovarian function decline)
avoid: Routine bacterial culture (unless resistant organisms or complicated infection are suspected)
Unnecessary combination of broad-spectrum antibiotics
Excessively invasive biopsy procedures (when there is no clear indication)

first_line: Topical estrogen therapy is preferred, such as estriol cream or promestriene vaginal capsules, once nightly for 2 weeks, then reduced to 2-3 times per week for maintenance. Lactobacillus preparations are used to regulate the vaginal microbiota. Nonpharmacologic interventions include keeping the vulva clean and dry, avoiding irritating washes, and using lubricants during sexual intercourse. The course usually needs to continue for several months to improve mucosal atrophy.
safety_warnings: Estrogens are contraindicated in patients with a history of breast cancer or endometrial cancer.
In unexplained vaginal bleeding, malignancy must be excluded before medication can be used.
Be alert to thromboembolic risk; long-term users require regular monitoring.
personalization: Patients with diabetes require strict glycemic control to prevent secondary infection.
In patients with hepatic impairment, oral estrogens should be used cautiously, with topical administration preferred.
In individuals at high risk of thrombosis, the benefit-risk ratio should be rigorously assessed.

skills.presentation: Patients are mostly more than 2 weeks postpartum, complaining of persistently incomplete or heavy lochia, with the color changing from pale red to bright red or dark red, accompanied by clots. They often describe lower abdominal bearing-down fullness, dull pain, or backache; when the uterine fundus is palpated, there is marked pain and the uterine body is soft and enlarged, located higher than expected. Some patients have low-grade fever or generalized fatigue, and vigilance for secondary infection is required.

first_questions: How long has it been since you gave birth? How have the color and amount of your lochia changed compared with just after delivery?
Do you have lower abdominal bearing-down pain or backache? How severe is the pain?
followup_questions: Does the lochia have a foul odor or contain large clots?
Have you recently had fever, chills, dizziness, or fatigue?
stop_conditions: The duration of lochia has been clearly established as exceeding the normal range and is accompanied by typical signs such as abdominal pain and uterine fundal tenderness.
Other clear causes such as retained placental fragments and puerperal infection have been excluded.
The patient's vital signs are stable, with no signs of acute hemorrhagic shock.

essential: Gynecologic bimanual examination (to assess uterine size, consistency, tenderness, and position)
Transvaginal ultrasonography (to screen for intrauterine retained products and fluid)
Complete blood count (to assess infection markers and degree of anemia)
if_suspected: Complete coagulation panel (to exclude bleeding due to coagulation disorders)
C-reactive protein and procalcitonin (to differentiate whether severe infection is present)
Urine HCG testing (to exclude gestational trophoblastic disease)
avoid: Blind diagnostic curettage (perforation is likely before retained pregnancy products are excluded)
Routine use of potent hemostatic agents without identifying the cause
Unnecessary pelvic CT (radiation risk and lower soft-tissue resolution than ultrasound)

first_line: First-line treatment is intravenous infusion or intramuscular injection of oxytocin to promote uterine contraction, along with Chinese patent medicines such as Motherwort granules to assist in expelling blood stasis. If infection is present, broad-spectrum antibiotics (such as cephalosporins + metronidazole) should be used in combination. During treatment, encourage the mother to breastfeed early to stimulate endogenous oxytocin secretion, and advise moderate activity to promote lochia drainage. The course is usually 3-7 days, until uterine involution returns to normal size and lochia turns white.
safety_warnings: Potent uterotonic agents must not be used alone when the placenta has not completely separated or retained products are present, to prevent tissue entrapment.
Monitor blood pressure changes; oxytocin overdose may cause hypotension or water intoxication.
If high fever or severe abdominal pain occurs, stop the drug immediately and reassess for endometritis or sepsis.
personalization: After cesarean delivery, be alert to poor incisional healing; drug doses should be adjusted according to body weight and hepatic and renal function.
For breastfeeding women, prefer drugs safe for the infant and avoid preparations that affect milk secretion.
In patients with a history of hypertension, use oxytocin cautiously; ergonovine (with blood pressure monitoring) or traditional Chinese medicine may be used instead.

skills.presentation: Patients often present with increased menstrual bleeding, prolonged menses, or irregular vaginal bleeding, and some have anemia symptoms. They may experience lower abdominal fullness or pressure symptoms such as urinary frequency and constipation. Gynecologic examination may reveal an enlarged uterus with a smooth surface but firm consistency, and a mass may be seen protruding through the cervical os.

first_questions: Are your menstrual cycles regular? Has your menstrual flow increased significantly?
Have you recently had irregular vaginal bleeding or symptoms of anemia (such as dizziness or fatigue)?
followup_questions: If you have abnormal bleeding, is it related to sexual intercourse or strenuous exercise?
Do you have lower abdominal pain or pressure symptoms (such as urinary frequency or constipation)?
stop_conditions: The patient has clearly described typical menstrual abnormalities and anemia symptoms and has no other complex medical history.
The patient has provided a complete menstrual history and prior gynecologic examination results.
The patient indicates that no further questioning is needed, and the symptoms are consistent with common presentations.

essential: Transvaginal ultrasonography
Complete blood count
Pelvic MRI (if necessary)
if_suspected: Hysteroscopy
Diagnostic curettage
Tumor marker testing (e.g., CA125)
avoid: Routine X-ray examination (low soft-tissue resolution)
Unnecessary radionuclide scanning
Laparoscopic exploration without an indication

first_line: First-line treatment includes medical therapy (such as GnRH agonists to reduce fibroid volume) and surgical treatment (hysteroscopic myomectomy). For asymptomatic small fibroids, regular follow-up may be used. The course of medication is usually 3-6 months, and the appropriate surgical approach should be selected according to fibroid size and location. After surgery, attention should be paid to preventing infection and bleeding.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of GnRH agonists, which can lead to osteoporosis
Assess coagulation function before surgery to prevent the risk of intraoperative bleeding
Be alert for postoperative intrauterine adhesions or infectious complications
personalization: For women of reproductive age, prioritize surgical approaches that preserve fertility
Postmenopausal women without symptoms may be managed with conservative observation
Patients with anemia should receive iron supplementation and have hemoglobin levels monitored

skills.presentation: Patients often present with tall stature, hypotonia, or delayed motor development, and some have learning disabilities or delayed language development. Gynecologically, most patients have normal menarche, but they may show oligomenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, or signs of diminished ovarian function. Some patients have a history of recurrent spontaneous abortion or a complaint of infertility. Typical signs include mild intellectual disability, seizures, or urogenital malformations, but many adult patients are not identified early because symptoms are subtle.

first_questions: Have you had multiple spontaneous abortions or unexplained infertility?
Have you or your child had significant growth and developmental delay, learning difficulties, or delayed language development?
Is there a family history of similar chromosomal abnormalities or recurrent miscarriage?
followup_questions: If you have menstrual abnormalities, are they specifically prolonged cycles, reduced menstrual flow, or amenorrhea?
Have you ever had unexplained seizures or severe behavioral and emotional problems?
Have you previously undergone chromosomal karyotype analysis or other genetic testing?
stop_conditions: When a diagnosis of 47,XXX has been clearly established and there are no acute complications requiring management.
When the patient and family have sufficient understanding of the disease and no further genetic counseling is needed.
When the necessary fertility assessment has been completed and a follow-up plan has been developed.

essential: Peripheral blood lymphocyte chromosome karyotype analysis (G-banding)
Sex hormone six-item panel (FSH, LH, E2, etc.)
Pelvic ultrasonography (to assess uterine and ovarian morphology)
if_suspected: FMR1 gene methylation testing (to exclude overlapping fragile X syndrome)
Thyroid function testing (to evaluate accompanying endocrine abnormalities)
Electroencephalography (if there is a history of seizures)
avoid: Invasive prenatal diagnosis without an indication (e.g., amniocentesis) solely for screening purposes
Nontargeted whole-body CT scanning (radiation risk exceeds benefit)
Routine tumor marker screening (in the absence of specific clinical indications)

first_line: There is currently no specific curative treatment, and symptomatic supportive care is the main approach. For menstrual irregularities, short-term sequential estrogen-progestin therapy may be used to regulate the cycle

For patients with developmental delay, rehabilitation training and special education should be introduced as early as possible. Monitoring of sex hormone levels and bone mineral density every 6-12 months is recommended to prevent osteoporosis. Psychological support and genetic counseling are core interventions that help patients and families cope with potential learning and fertility challenges.
safety_warnings: Long-term estrogen replacement therapy requires vigilance for the risk of thrombosis, especially in patients with a smoking history or obesity.
Avoid indiscriminate use of ovulation induction drugs, which may increase the risk of multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.
Pay attention to drug interactions, especially the metabolic effects between antiepileptic drugs and hormonal drugs.
personalization: Women of reproductive age: ovarian reserve function should be assessed in detail before planning pregnancy, with assisted reproductive technology intervention if necessary.
Adolescent patients: focus on the height growth curve and development of secondary sexual characteristics, and initiate growth hormone assessment at the appropriate time.
Older patients: strengthen bone health management and regularly screen for the risk of breast and gynecologic malignancies.

skills.presentation: Patients often report that uterine enlargement is significantly faster than in a singleton pregnancy, severe nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy, and frequent fetal movements or abnormal abdominal distention in the middle and late trimesters. They may have dyspnea, worsening lower extremity edema, and symptoms of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. Watch for signs of preterm labor such as regular uterine contractions, vaginal bleeding, or rupture of membranes.

first_questions: What is your last menstrual period and estimated due date?
Is it known that you have a twin pregnancy? Is there a family history?
Have you recently had abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, or abnormal discharge?
followup_questions: If you have contractions, what is their frequency and duration?
Do you have headache, blurred vision, or other hypertension-related symptoms?
Do you have a history of miscarriage, preterm birth, or cesarean delivery?
stop_conditions: Twin type (chorionicity) and gestational age have been clearly determined
No acute complications and stable vital signs
Basic obstetric assessment and necessary tests have been completed

essential: Transvaginal ultrasonography (to determine chorionicity and fetal number)
Complete blood count and coagulation function testing
Blood pressure monitoring and urine protein testing
if_suspected: Glucose tolerance test (to screen for gestational diabetes mellitus)
Cervical length measurement (to assess preterm birth risk)
Fetal growth ultrasonography (to monitor growth discrepancy)
avoid: Routine X-ray examination (unless there is an emergency indication)
Unnecessary invasive procedures (such as amniocentesis)

first_line: First-line treatment includes regular prenatal visits (every 2-4 weeks), folic acid and iron supplementation, and nutritional support. Progesterone or magnesium sulfate may be used to prevent preterm birth. If preeclampsia occurs, blood pressure must be controlled and pregnancy should be terminated at the appropriate time. Planned delivery at 36-37 weeks is recommended to avoid complications caused by spontaneous labor.
safety_warnings: NSAIDs are contraindicated to prevent fetal renal impairment
Pay attention to drug interactions, especially between anticoagulants and antihypertensive drugs
Be alert for the risk of postpartum hemorrhage and prepare blood products in advance
personalization: For pregnant women of advanced maternal age, strengthen blood glucose and blood pressure monitoring
For multiple pregnancies, increase the iron dose to prevent anemia
Consider cervical cerclage in patients with a history of preterm birth

skills.presentation: Patients often seek care for infertility, recurrent spontaneous abortion, or preterm birth. Typical manifestations include regular menstrual cycles but possibly reduced menstrual flow, and some patients have cyclic lower abdominal pain (if there is a rudimentary horn with endometrium). During pregnancy, abnormal fetal presentation, placental abruption, and late miscarriage are likely to occur. Gynecologic examination may reveal asymmetric uterine morphology, with one uterine horn full and the other empty.

first_questions: Have you ever been pregnant? Specifically, was it a term delivery, miscarriage, or preterm birth?
Are your menstrual cycles regular? Has your menstrual flow changed significantly compared with before?
Have you had cyclic abdominal pain or unexplained infertility?
followup_questions: If you have had a miscarriage, at what gestational week did it occur? Was it accompanied by severe abdominal pain?
If you have abdominal pain, is the pain related to your menstrual cycle? Does it radiate to the lumbosacral region?
If you are planning pregnancy, have you previously undergone imaging tests related to uterine structure?
stop_conditions: The patient has clearly reported a history of infertility or recurrent miscarriage, and uterine malformation is highly suspected
The patient's reported symptoms are typical, and key reproductive history information has been provided
The patient refuses further examination or clearly states that only consultation is needed

essential: Three-dimensional ultrasonography (3D-US)
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), pelvic non-contrast plus contrast-enhanced
if_suspected: Hysteroscopy (to assess uterine cavity morphology and rudimentary horn status)
Laparoscopy (to confirm diagnosis and assess pelvic adhesions and fallopian tube status)
avoid: Routine X-ray hysterosalpingography (low soft-tissue resolution; not first-line)
Blind diagnostic curettage (increases the risk of injury when there is no indication)

first_line: Asymptomatic patients do not require special treatment and can undergo regular follow-up. If a functional rudimentary horn causes dysmenorrhea or hematometra, laparoscopic resection of the rudimentary horn should be performed. For those with fertility needs, uterine cavity morphology should be assessed before pregnancy

During pregnancy, strengthen monitoring, prevent preterm birth, and perform cervical cerclage if necessary. After delivery, pay attention to contraception to avoid the increased risk associated with unintended pregnancy.
safety_warnings: Induced abortion is strictly prohibited before rudimentary horn pregnancy has been excluded, to prevent uterine rupture
When using tocolytic agents during pregnancy, closely monitor fetal heart rate and maternal blood pressure
Surgical procedures should avoid injury to adjacent ureters and blood vessels
personalization: For young nulliparous women, prioritize minimally invasive surgical approaches that preserve fertility
For older patients or those with severe complications, multidisciplinary consultation is needed to develop an individualized delivery plan
For patients with other reproductive tract malformations, related anatomic abnormalities should be managed concurrently

skills.presentation: Patients complain of single or multiple painless masses on the vulva, varying in size, which may slowly enlarge over time. Some patients develop local redness and swelling, severe pain, and marked tenderness due to cyst infection or rupture, and may even have fever and difficulty walking. The skin over the mass may be red; if it is a Bartholin gland cyst, it is usually located in the posterior part of the labium majus; if it is a sebaceous cyst, it is mostly located in hair follicle-bearing areas, with a central black dot visible.

first_questions: How long have you had the vulvar lump, and has it grown rapidly recently?
Do you have pain, redness, swelling, or warmth at the lump?
Have you recently had trauma or childbirth, or do you have a history of similar masses?
followup_questions: If you have pain, does it affect urination or walking?
Has the mass ever ruptured on its own, draining pus or blood?
Have you had a history of high-risk sexual contact or recurrent vaginitis?
stop_conditions: The location, size, consistency, and presence or absence of fluctuance of the mass have been determined.
It has been confirmed that there are no acute systemic infection symptoms (such as high fever or chills).
High-risk factors related to malignancy (such as induration or fixation) have been excluded.

essential: Gynecologic bimanual examination
Inspection and palpation of the vulva
Gram stain of discharge smear
if_suspected: Pelvic ultrasonography
Cytologic examination of cyst aspirate
Complete blood count and C-reactive protein testing
avoid: Blind incision and drainage of an undiagnosed solid mass
Routine use of broad-spectrum antibiotics without an indication of infection
Unnecessary extensive biopsy in young women

first_line: Asymptomatic small cysts can be observed and followed up. When symptomatic or infected, incision and drainage with placement of a Word catheter for marsupialization is preferred, leaving it in place for 2–4 weeks to prevent recurrence. If infection is present, oral antibiotics (such as a cephalosporin combined with metronidazole) are needed for 5–7 days. Noninfected cysts can be treated with laser marsupialization or cyst excision. After surgery, keep the vulva clean and avoid friction.
safety_warnings: Never forcibly squeeze the cyst without anesthesia to prevent spread of infection.
Pay attention to the history of drug allergy, especially to penicillins and cephalosporins.
Be alert to the risk of sepsis caused by abscess formation, and monitor body temperature closely.
personalization: For pregnant patients, conservative treatment or simple drainage under local anesthesia is preferred, and general anesthesia should be avoided.
For patients with diabetes, strengthen glycemic control and prolong the antibiotic course to prevent recurrence.
For postmenopausal women, if the cyst persists, be alert to the possibility of malignant transformation; complete excision with pathologic examination is recommended.
